rss_0_1786061153.title: Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say
rss_0_1786061153.text:
The virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.

Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.

The Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was first reported on 15 May, although there are suspicions the disease could have been spreading since January.

There have been 3,973 cases and 1,801 deaths recorded as of 4 August, according to the DRC’s national public health institute. Speaking on Thursday, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told a press briefing cases had topped 4,000.

The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. There are eight times more cases, and six times more deaths than were recorded 11 weeks into the West Africa Ebola outbreak in 2014-18, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed at least 11,000.

Kaseya said he had spoken to the director general of the World Health Organization, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, and they planned studies “to check if there is no additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating. Because the level of severity of this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented.”

More than two-thirds of Ebola deaths are happening in the community rather than in treatment centres. In a treatment centre run by MSF in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, 90% of admitted patients do not appear on authorities’ lists of contacts of known cases. Both factors indicate high levels of untracked transmission.

Kaseya said contact tracing in the DRC was insufficient, with only 10 contacts identified for every Ebola patient, when about 40 would be the expected number.

Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever that can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, organ damage and internal bleeding. The outbreak is centred on the conflict-affected mining province of Ituri, but has spread to Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo. There were 20 cases recorded in neighbouring Uganda before it brought its outbreak under control.

Dr Wessam Mankoula, acting head of emergency preparedness and response at Africa CDC, said response teams planned a shift “from contact tracing to active case search”, which would mean community health workers “moving from door to door” asking households if they had anyone sick with Ebola symptoms.

He added: “I think the time for incremental action is over and we’re starting now the phase for scaling up.”

Kaseya promised a “village-centered response” that would involve communities, more use of digital tools and greater action in the camps for people who have been internally displaced by conflict in affected provinces.

Officials also said they planned to begin using antiviral remdesivir on a compassionate use basis to treat patients. They will also start testing whether Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for use against a different strain of Ebola, should be offered in the affected province, after receiving data suggesting that Bundibugyo caused less serious disease and “zero death” among people who had received that jab.

“Seeing the expansion of this outbreak, only the public health measure will not be enough to quickly control or stop this outbreak,” said Dr Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC director of research, clinical trials and innovation.

DRC authorities said they were investigating a suspected Ebola death on a boat heading to the capital, Kinshasa, from the north-east of the country, and that the other passengers on board would be quarantined and tested.

Unicef warned that essential healthcare was being disrupted by the outbreak as fear of infection and service disruptions kept families away from clinics. In the outbreak’s centre, the mining town of Mongbwalu, the proportion of children receiving their first measles dose has fallen 69%.

rss_1_1786061153.title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
rss_1_1786061153.text:
The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.

The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada.

The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants.

More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association.

Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China.

“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee.

“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?”

The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods.

Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital.

Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests.

“I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto.

“It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.”

A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.”

China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”.

A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time.

“We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.”

In a later statement, issued after this story was first published, a department spokesperson countered the assertion that the closures would benefit China.

“Claims that China is filling a diplomatic vacuum is [sic] inherently false and we recommend that individuals who subscribe to this propaganda take a look at the so-called help China had in the recent earthquakes in Venezuela or to address the Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson said.

The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions.

Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

rss_2_1786061153.title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones
rss_2_1786061153.text:
The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.

David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.

Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital, where he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.

Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious, the BBC reported.

Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.

He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.

He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations.

SC Villa said: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”

The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associations said: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”

It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.”

The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.

In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.

Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”

rss_3_1786061154.title: Nigerian security forces free more than 300 hostages in ‘largest single-day recovery’
rss_3_1786061154.text:
Nigerian security forces have rescued more than 300 abducted people in what the president, Bola Ahmed Tinubu, hailed as the largest single-day hostage recovery in the country’s history.

The release was announced on Wednesday after a joint operation, conducted by the military, police and counter-terrorism units, freed victims held captive in the dense forests of the Kainji Lake national park in the north-central region.

Among those who regained freedom were 163 people abducted in February during a deadly raid on the village of Woro in Kwara state, and 145 others seized primarily from the neighbouring Niger state. Both states are flanked to the west by Benin, where militant attacks have been surging in recent times. Officials confirmed the survivors are receiving medical evaluations at an army installation before being reunited with their families.

View image in fullscreen A woman walks past debris, burnt structures and damaged shops after the February attack on Woro. Photograph: Light Oriye Tamunotonye/AFP/Getty Images

“The successful execution of this intelligence-led operation demonstrates the growing efficiency and collaboration among our security services,” Tinubu said in a statement on the presidency’s website. “I commend our gallant men and women in uniform for their bravery and unwavering commitment to safeguarding Nigerian lives.”

The government spokesperson Bayo Onanuga said the rescue operation was part of the president’s resolve to “restore lasting peace across every corner of the nation”.

In the last decade, kidnapping for ransom has become endemic in Africa’s most populous country, especially in the north where different armed groups including bandit gangs and jihadists roam large unoccupied forests and shrublands.

Between July 2024 and June 2025, at least 4,722 people were kidnapped across 997 reported incidents, leading to at least 762 deaths, according to a report by the Lagos-based geopolitical advisory SBM Intelligence. In that 12-month period, abductors demanded ₦48bn ($35m or £26m) in payments, with families and communities ultimately handing over at least ₦2.57bn in ransom to secure the release of their loved ones.

Ahead of January’s presidential election in which Tinubu is seeking a second four-year term, the government has been ramping up reforms and rescue operations as insecurity worsens.

The latest rescue was announced in the same week the army declared the governor of Islamic State West Africa Province, Abu Musa al-Mangawi Baa Shuwa, and his deputy, Amirul Jaish Muhammad Jidda, wanted. The duo run the Islamic State-affiliated Boko Haram offshoot operating primarily around the Lake Chad basin, which straddles Cameroon, Chad, Niger and Nigeria.

View image in fullscreen Teachers and students went to Lagos in June to call for the release of those abducted from a school in Oyo state. Security services freed at least 40 students and teachers in July. Photograph: Emmanuel Adegboye/EPA

In July, security services freed at least 40 students and teachers who had been kidnapped in May from a school in Oyo in south-western Nigeria.

Last week, the presidency announced a salary increase worth 30% to 80% for thousands of soldiers, the largest hike in years for an army once seen as one of the continent’s most powerful but now derided as underfunded and unequipped to handle concurrent insurgencies across Nigerian territory.

rss_4_1786061154.title: ‘Morocco feels emboldened’: Trump’s influence in spotlight after Ceuta disaster
rss_4_1786061154.text:
The cosy relationship between Washington and Rabat has long been flaunted by both sides, from Morocco’s announcement this year that it would be the first African state to join Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to the congratulatory message recently sent by Trump to mark King Mohammed VI’s 27 years in power.

The latest example landed this week. As Spain grappled with the aftermath of the sudden influx – and swift return – of more than 70,000 people into Ceuta, Morocco’s monarch confirmed he had named a $1bn highway flanking the disputed territory of Western Sahara after Trump.

The deepening ties have come under renewed scrutiny as questions continue to swirl over what exactly led to the deadly mass border crossing into the tiny Spanish territory in north Africa.

“I think there’s enough evidence to hypothesise or claim that Morocco is behind this,” said Riccardo Fabiani, the north Africa project director for the International Crisis Group. “But there was no clear trigger for this, and this is what is puzzling for everyone.”

0:44 Migrants in Spain’s Ceuta enclave escorted back to Morocco – video

Observers have suggested Spain’s recent rapprochement with Rabat’s archrival, Algeria, could have set off Morocco. But another, perhaps more plausible explanation pointed towards the US, said Fabiani.

“It’s obviously impossible to demonstrate,” he said. “But in terms of plausibility, I don’t think it’s impossible to imagine that Morocco might have done something to earn brownie points with its allies, given that Morocco and this particular administration in Washington do have a very close, excellent relationship.”

While Morocco had probably not “masterminded” the surge into Ceuta, he said, its relationship with the Trump administration – along with the Moroccan king’s desire to keep its claim to Ceuta in the spotlight – may have affected how it responded to fast-spreading online rumours about the Spanish border being thrown open.

View image in fullscreen A young person is escorted by Spanish security forces after attempting to cross into Ceuta on Saturday. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters

“For sure the Moroccan security forces were monitoring those conversations,” said Fabiani. “They saw that and there was probably some conversation where they decided to do nothing and see where this goes.”

What followed made headlines across the globe as tens of thousands of people swam or waded across one of the EU’s two land borders with Africa. As Spain scrambled to cope, far-right voices seized on the images.

In the US, the vice-president, JD Vance, and the state department blamed the influx on the Socialist-led government of Spain, while Trump warned that electing Democrats would make what happened in Spain “look small-time”. At no point did any of them mention Morocco or the potential role it might have played.

Trump and his administration have long been open about the deep antipathy they feel for Pedro Sánchez, the Spanish prime minister, whose refusal to allow the US to use its airbases during the Iran war, rejection of the 5% defence spending target and vociferous criticism of Israel’s actions in Gaza have arguably made Spain the administration’s least favourite EU country.

The American response seemed to be a triumph for Rabat, whose relationship with the US president traces back to his first term, when Morocco agreed to normalise ties with Israel in exchange for Trump’s recognition of its sovereignty claim over the disputed territory of Western Sahara.

Since then, Morocco’s all-powerful monarch had doubled down on outreach efforts, said Fabiani. “The Moroccans have really made extra efforts to cultivate every single major decision-maker within the administration, including the president himself, to make sure that this administration will support, until the end, the Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara.”

A hint that the relationship could help Morocco lay claim to more than Western Sahara came in a recent US congressional report that appeared to be sympathetic to Morocco’s refusal to recognise Ceuta as Spanish territory, describing it as “Spanish-administered” rather than a part of Spain, as it has been since 1580.

Days after the influx, interest in Ceuta remained heightened among those close to both Trump and the Israeli government, said Haizam Amirah-Fernández, the director of the Madrid-based Centre for Contemporary Arab Studies. “They haven’t stopped talking about Ceuta for several days in a row, which is quite striking.”

View image in fullscreen Red Cross personnel distributing food at Trampolín beach in Ceuta this week. Photograph: REDUAN/EPA

What had been laid bare was Rabat’s willingness to use “hybrid tactics to achieve political objectives”, said Amirah-Fernández, drawing a parallel with May 2021 when Rabat loosened border controls to allow more than 8,000 people to cross into Ceuta in a show of anger over Madrid’s decision to allow a Western Sahara pro-independence leader to travel to Spain to be treated for Covid-19.

This time around, as nearly 10 times more people crossed into Ceuta, it set off a bout of finger-pointing across the EU rather than any kind of concerted effort to push back using the bloc’s status as Morocco’s largest trading partner and largest foreign investor. “The reaction of several governments in the EU was, in the end, what the White House was looking for – the erosion of solidarity between European partners,” said Amirah-Fernández.

Senior officials in Morocco have pushed back against accusations it was in any way complicit.

View image in fullscreen King Mohammed VI and Trump in 2018. Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images

At the Rabat-based Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis, there was little doubt that relations between Morocco and the US were in their “golden era”. Even so, the country’s approach to the Trump administration remained pragmatic, said Said Saddiki, a senior fellow at the institute.

“Moroccan policymakers are well aware of President Trump’s transactional style and have sought to preserve Morocco’s strategic autonomy,” Saddiki said in an email, citing efforts to maintain partnerships with the EU, China and the Gulf states, among others.

“The relationship with the Trump administration has strengthened Morocco’s international position, but so far it has not come at the expense of its relations with Spain or the European Union.”

For Fabiani, the events in Ceuta served to underscore the perils of Europe’s reliance on north African states to control migration flows. “This has made Europe entirely vulnerable and dependent on the goodwill of a country like Morocco,” he said. “Morocco is a partner, but at the same time it has its own interests. This vulnerability was on show.”

This weakness could become more of an issue as time passed, given Morocco’s perception that the issue of Ceuta remained unsettled, Fabiani warned. “And Morocco feels emboldened, and there is an administration in Washington that is willing to back it up,” he said. “I don’t think Europe is ready for what comes next because it could get much more complicated.”

rss_5_1786061154.title: Toronto zoo announces birth of pygmy hippo calf, third for mother Kindia
rss_5_1786061154.text:
The Toronto Zoo has announced the birth of a female pygmy hippo calf.

Kindia, the zoo’s 20-year-old pygmy hippo, started showing signs of labor at around 8.15am last Sunday, it said. Around four hours later, the calf’s feet emerged and after 1.5 hours of active labor, Kindia successfully gave birth to the baby pygmy hippo.

Within 15 minutes of birth, the calf began trying to stand and was “confidently navigating the space” a few hours later, the zoo said, adding that the calf was seen nursing approximately 4.5 hours after birth.

The zoo has not identified the calf yet, but said that it is doing well alongside its mother. According to the zoo, the newborn is Kindia’s third calf. Kindia became pregnant after she was introduced to a 31-year-old male pygmy hippo named Harvey for eight days in January.

“This wonderful news comes with both hope and caution,” the zoo said. “Kindia successfully raised her daughter Penelope in 2018, and calf survival for this species can be challenging. Our team will continue to closely monitor both mom and calf around the clock during these important first days to ensure they continue to progress well together.”

Noting the species’ endangered status on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list, Dolf DeJong, the Toronto Zoo’s CEO, said: “Welcoming a pygmy hippo calf is far more than a celebration of new life. Pygmy hippos are endangered, and their wild populations continue to decline due to habitat loss and human pressures.

“This birth represents the critical role modern accredited zoos play in conservation, scientific collaboration, and maintaining healthy populations that contribute to the long-term survival of the species.”

Only approximately 2,000 to 3,000 pygmy hippos are believed to remain in the wild.

With adult pygmy hippos weighing anywhere from 330lb to 660lb and standing around 2.5ft tall, the species are native to the forests and swamps of west Africa. In recent decades however, pygmy hippos have faced growing threats to their habitat including logging, mining, farming activities as well as human settlement.

rss_6_1786061154.title: Mexican influencer shot dead while streaming live on social media
rss_6_1786061154.text:
A popular Mexican influencer has been shot dead while doing a live stream on social media outside a restaurant in Sinaloa state, where lethal cartel violence has become widespread.

César Gastélum, who had nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok and was known for making comedy videos, was filming with two friends outside a fast-food restaurant in the city of Culiacán. The three were dressed in the bright orange jackets and backpacks of food delivery drivers.

A motorcycle with a driver and pillion rider suddenly pulled up beside them and the driver pulled out a gun and shot Gastélum at point-blank range.

A security official in Sinaloa confirmed Gastélum’s death to Reuters and said a major security operation was under way.

The killing is the latest example of bloodshed in Culiacán, which has become an epicentre of violence as factions of the Sinaloa cartel battle for control of the city.

View image in fullscreen Onlookers stand behind a police cordon at the scene of César Gastélum’s killing Photograph: Jesús Bustamante/Reuters

Mexico’s security cabinet wrote on X that it was investigating several of Gastélum’s posts, “some of which referred to a faction of a criminal group”. It also said video surveillance footage and other evidence were being analysed to identify and apprehend those responsible.

Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, said on Wednesday that authorities were investigating the killing and working to identify the killer.

“The actual perpetrators, and if applicable the mastermind, must be arrested, and the reason behind this tragic homicide must be uncovered,” she said in her morning press conference.

At least 12 social media influencers have been murdered in Culiacán since two factions of the Sinaloa cartel began their battle in September 2024, according to local media.

They have also been targeted in Jalisco state. Valeria Márquez, 23, was shot and killed at a beauty salon last year while live-streaming on TikTok, where she had thousands of followers.

Authorities announced last week that they had arrested Ramón Ángel Álvarez Ayala, the leader of a criminal cell with links to the Jalisco New Generation cartel, in relation to the killing.

They also accused him of ordering and financing the November 2025 assassination of Carlos Manzo, the mayor of Uruapan, the second largest city in Michoacán state, in a killing that shocked the country.

rss_7_1786061155.title: Peruvian cardinal hails $150m lead poisoning settlement for 1,300 people as a ‘historic milestone’
rss_7_1786061155.text:
A Peruvian cardinal who received a barrage of death threats when he challenged the firm behind a toxic smelter has called a $150m (£111m) out-of-court settlement to more than 1,000 people who were allegedly poisoned by the plant as children “a historic milestone”.

Cardinal Pedro Barreto, 82, was in Rome meeting Pope Leo XIV and other cardinals in June when he received news that the firm that ran the smelter, the Doe Run Company, a subsidiary of Renco Group, would pay $150m to 1,373 Peruvians who have suffered health impacts since childhood.

View image in fullscreen Cardinal Pedro Barreto led a campaign for justice for the Andean town of La Oroya. Photograph: Andrew Medichini/AP

The news came as Barreto – the former archbishop of Huancayo, a city in the Peruvian Andes – was preparing to travel to the US to testify in the first of four civil trials in St Louis, Missouri, as part of a 19-year legal battle against Doe Run, which is owned by US billionaire Ira Rennert, who also serves as chair of the Renco Group.

“This is a historic milestone,” said Barreto, speaking to the Guardian. “But this long-awaited justice doesn’t solve the problem faced by many children who were personally affected, especially neurologically. The money will not compensate for the harm they have suffered, but it is a sign that justice has been served.”

Barreto led a nearly two-decade campaign to hold the US company to account for the severe health impacts on the population of the Andean town of La Oroya, which the Blacksmith Institute, a US-based environmental NGO now known as Pure Earth, in 2007 listed as one of the world’s 10 most polluted places.

The settlement brought to a close one of the longest-running civil lawsuits against a multinational corporation in one country for environmental pollution or toxic exposure that caused injury or damage in another country.

Schlichter Bogard, a St Louis-based law firm, alleged that Doe Run failed to reduce lead emissions at the Peruvian multi-metal smelter, resulting in permanent injuries and harm. Doe Run Resources Corporation, which has its headquarters in St Louis, did not admit wrongdoing in agreeing to the settlement.

What began in 2007 in state court on behalf of 17 Peruvian children grew into a federal court case with more than 1,373 plaintiffs, now young adults. Each could receive at least $100,000 from the payout.

Jerry Schlichter, the founder and co-managing partner of the law firm, described the payout as a “historic tipping point in that the American companies in this case have been held responsible for their actions in another country to foreign citizens who are not US residents”.

View image in fullscreen An aerial image of the Doe Run complex and the town of La Oroya in 2022. Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty Images

Schlichter said his team of lawyers and religious leaders such as Barreto won the settlement because of their “passion and conviction that this was a just cause, this was a righteous battle”, and that the individuals deserved their compensation for the exposure to lead emissions.

“This will be a life-changing event for every one of these 1,373 children,” Schlichter said. “It will enable them to have a new path in their life, whatever that might be.”

During his time as archbishop of Huancayo, Barreto had contacted the Saint Louis University College for Public Health and Social Justice, which sent researchers to assess the affected children in La Oroya in 2005 and found they had among some of the highest blood lead levels ever recorded. The university also found that lead, arsenic, cadmium and sulphur dioxide emissions had increased since Doe Run took over the smelting complex in 1997.

Nearly 100% of children under the age of six in La Oroya had blood-lead levels above 10 μg/dL (10 micrograms of lead in every tenth of a litre of blood), well in excess of levels that can cause growth impairment and lower IQs in children, according to a 2004 study by Peru’s environmental health office.

Barreto faced death threats and harassment, often from employees at the smelter who feared losing their livelihoods, after he began his activism in 2004, soon after taking on the archdiocese of Huancayo that includes La Oroya.

“It was an irrefutable fact that I was threatened in various ways,” said Barreto, one of three Peruvian cardinals. He said it was often done publicly and through messages that indicated that “if I kept speaking out, they were going to take much more drastic measures”.

But he stressed that it was the local population who deserved recognition.

“We have had to endure just a little of the immense suffering they constantly face,” he said.

“Before settlement, it was the longest-running case in the federal court system,” said Schlichter, who said it had been a David v Goliath fight against Rennert. “Tens of thousands of attorney hours were spent on the case and we had five national law firms who were opposing us,” he said.

View image in fullscreen Mothers wait with their children for a medical examination at La Oroya’s health clinic, 2013. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

The Department of Justice joined the defendants in asking that the lawsuit be transferred to Peru, but Schlichter resolutely opposed. “If the case had gone to Peru, the children would have got nothing,” he said. Winning the settlement was “very gratifying after such a long and risky fight”, he added.

The New York-based Renco Group and its founder, Rennert, 92, made a fortune in the 1980s junk-bond market before developing an empire of mining companies, smelting plants and industrial firms. According to Forbes in 2024, his worth is estimated at $3.8bn (£2.8bn).

In a statement, Doe Run’s chief executive, Matt Wohl, said: “We elected to put this behind us and focus on what matters – running our business, serving our customers and investing in new technologies.”

rss_8_1786061155.title: Mexico’s top university orders 58,000 students to resit entrance exam after suspected cheating
rss_8_1786061155.text:
Mexico’s largest and most prestigious university has announced that about 58,000 students will have to resit their entrance exam after abnormally high test results raised suspicions of widespread cheating.

The National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam) said the exam would take place in person after its first attempt at a fully remote online version led to a debacle and thousands of annulled results.

“The Unam, the home of science, humanities and understanding, knows how to recognie mistakes and self-correct,” the university’s rector, Leonardo Lomelí, said on Monday. “There is no evasion or complacency. There is responsibility and we act accordingly.”

Nearly 160,000 students took the entrance exam earlier this summer. The at-home test included an AI-powered webcam to monitor candidates with voice and facial recognition to ensure no cheating took place. But the results indicated that the checks had failed to stop fraud.

Between 2021 and 2025 only 3.5% of applicants obtained a score of 100 or more out of 120, but this year the figure was 16%. The proportion of students who achieved a score of 110 or more increased sixfold from 0.9% to 5.5%.

Almost 30% of candidates for the medicine programme, among the most competitive undergraduate tracks in the region, obtained a score of 100 or more, compared with 9% last year.

View image in fullscreen Unam’s central library in Mexico City. Photograph: David R Frazier Photolibrary, Inc./Alamy

The results sparked a national scandal, leading the country’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, to suggest the country’s attorney general may have to investigate. “Support is always available, but in any case if a crime has been committed it is a matter for the prosecutor’s office,” she said.

Hundreds of Unam applicants protested in Mexico City on Monday against having to take the control exam, blocking major thoroughfares in the south of the capital.

Lomelí said: “I offer an apology to the candidates who, having been fairly accepted, will be called upon to take the control exam. However, it is necessary to ensure certainty and guarantee equity in access.”

The drive for more equitable access led the university to offer the exam online for the first time this year. Students previously had to travel to Mexico City from their home states, sometimes many hundreds of miles away.

The entrance exam is notoriously competitive. The more than 150,000 applicants this year were competing for 21,962 places.

Just before the results were to be publicly released, the university announced it had annulled the results of 2% of tests – 3,174 exams – after detecting irregularities such as identity impersonation, external assistance and the use of AI.

A technical expert who reviewed the results told the New York Times (NYT) that nearly half of the exams – 75,000 tests – could have involved some degree of cheating. AI may have played a role, but test questions were also leaked and even sold online while the exam was open in May and June.

Cheating tips were also widely passed around before the test went live, according to the NYT.

The Unam announced in July that it had filed a criminal complaint after detecting the alleged irregularities. It said authorities would investigate potential misconduct involving individuals or companies that allegedly offered fraudulent services to applicants and their families.

The cheating scandal compelled the institution to halt all admissions and appoint a technical committee to decide the fate of the 158,712 young people who took the exam, an unprecedented measure in the university’s 115-year modern history.

Lomelí also announced that the academic year for new students would begin on 31 August, rather than 10 August as originally scheduled.

rss_9_1786061155.title: US revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feud
rss_9_1786061155.text:
Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The US state department said Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti’s visa had been cancelled in retaliation for Brazil’s refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília and its decision last month to deny visas to two US diplomats seeking to visit ahead of an October election.

The Trump administration stopped short of expelling Viotti, a former senior United Nations official. But Washington warned that further diplomatic action remains possible if Brasília continues to withhold its approval for would-be ambassador Daniel Perez, a Florida Republican and close ally of the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.

“We communicated continually with the Brazilian government for weeks and have given the Brazilian government every opportunity to do the right thing, yet they have continually delayed and obfuscated,” a state department spokesperson said.

The ambassador’s visa could be restored if Brazil accepts Perez’s appointment. “This is a reciprocal action,” the spokesperson said. “Should the ambassador leave the country, she would need to reapply for a visa.”

The dispute has become entangled with Brazil’s increasingly bitter election campaign, in which Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, and a close political ally of Trump.

Brasília swiftly condemned the US action as part of a deliberate campaign to influence the election. Lula’s office said: “Today’s decision is not an isolated incident. It is part of a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, motivated by ideological reasons.”

Brazil also accused the US of breaching diplomatic norms by announcing Perez’s nomination before seeking Brasília’s consent. The Brazilian government said its consideration of the appointment was still under way, and that it had been made clear no decision would be taken before the first round of the election, on 4 October.

The Trump administration argues that Brazil has no right to interfere with the president’s choice of US ambassador to the country.

“President Trump has the right to determine who represents the American people and interests around the world,” the state department said. “We reject any effort by foreign countries to interfere in our domestic processes.”

The latest confrontation follows Brazil’s refusal last month to issue visas to Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, and one of his senior aides.

The US officials had planned to visit Brasília from 27 to 30 July for meetings with government officials, religious leaders and others about election integrity, religious freedom and freedom of expression.

Washington described the trip as routine, and rejected Brazilian claims that it was intended to interfere in the election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” the state department said at the time.

Brasília has stood by its decision, saying the officials intended to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazil’s electronic voting system in what it called an “unacceptable attempt to interfere in the national political process”.

The row is particularly sensitive because Jair Bolsonaro and his supporters have spent years alleging, without evidence, that Brazil’s electronic voting system is vulnerable to fraud. He has been barred from standing for office and was convicted over a plot to overturn his defeat in the 2022 election.

The diplomatic confrontation is the latest in a series of clashes between Trump and Lula, whose governments have sharply diverged over Latin American politics, Venezuela, Cuba and the role of the US in the region.

Trump has repeatedly intervened in political contests across Latin America, while Lula has made national sovereignty a central theme of his campaign. The Brazilian president has blamed Rubio for some of the administration’s actions against his government, although he has sought to avoid a direct personal confrontation with Trump, and has said the two men got on well when they first met.

Economic pressure has added to the tensions. The Trump administration has imposed tariffs of up to 37.5% on thousands of Brazilian exports, citing what it says are unfair trade practices and failures to prevent forced labour. Lula’s government has rejected the allegations, and accused Trump’s administration of trying to help Bolsonaro’s political family.

The US has also classified Brazil’s two biggest drug-trafficking organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, a move opposed by Lula’s government.

Yet the state department insists that it still wants to restore a normal relationship with Brasília. “We want to be back in a situation where we have a normal, productive, transparent relationship with our colleagues,” a senior US official said.
